=== 26 June 2026 JB Final Brief.docx ===
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES

BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
 POST HEARING OF MERITS REPLY BRIEF OF INTERVENOR JOHN M. BURROW
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
I, John M. Burrow, Pro Se Intervenor, Party No. 811, Private Landowner, Route Links G71, G72, and G73, Bell County, Texas, file this final post hearing reply brief in opposition to the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation. I am not writing this as a lawyer. I have no training as a lawyer.  I am writing this as a fellow Texan, as a Bell County private landowner, as an engineer, as a small business owner, and as one of the people whose property, home, family, business, and community are being asked to carry the burden of a 765-kV project that the Applicants still have not proven is needed in the way they claim.  Their claim is of one of misdirection; of misinformation, and of misrepresentation; all to the disadvantage of the pubic.  
The Applicants are asking the Administrative Law Judges and the Commission to accept their misdirection, misinformation, and misrepresentation instead of proof. They say ERCOT already decided need. They say HB 5066 mandates this. They say the Public Utility Commission has requested their application. They say notice was sufficient. They say they exceeded the number of public meetings required. They say they have informed all affected landowners.  They say community values have been met. They say prudent avoidance was satisfied. They say they all statutory and administrative codes have been met. They say due rights have been met. But when those statements are tested against this record and evidence, they do not hold. The Applicants pat themselves on the back for doing a fine job, but what they have done is lay the burden of proof and billions in costs on the backs of Texas landowners and ratepayers.  
This case is not about whether the Permian Basin needs reliable power. It does. Everyone agrees Texas needs reliable power. This case is about whether these Applicants proved that this specific Bell County East to Big Hill to Sand Lake 765-kV line, Import Path 2, on this record, through these routes, under this notice process, should be approved now with the power of eminent domain, the government’s authority to seize private property without owners consent. They have not proved anything but one failed action, one failed step after another.
The record shows a fundamental problem at every level: the need was not quantified, the project timing was not established, HB 5066 was stretched beyond its text, alternatives were not fairly evaluated, public meetings were denied to approximately 1,400 newly affected landowners, current county tax rolls were not properly used, important community values were not obtained, late-noticed landowners were forced into a compressed process, habitable structure data was unreliable, and prudent avoidance was reduced to a spreadsheet instead of an actual effort to protect people.
Approving this project on this record would be like opening a bridge to the public after learning the engineer never finished the load calculations, structural beams were never inspected, and warnings from the people living below were ignored. When the consequences are permanent, the proof must be complete.
For those reasons, the Application for Docket 59182 and 59475 should be denied. At the very least, no route should be selected that crosses a landowner who was denied the public meeting opportunity required by 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) or who received application notice so late that meaningful participation was impaired.
TABLE OF CONTENTS
I. Introduction and Requested Relief
II. Governing Standards Under PURA and the Commission Rules
III. The Applicants Still Bear the Burden of Proof
IV. Reply to the Joint TSPs Response to the Legislators Amicus Brief
V. HB 5066 Does Not Mandate This 765-kV Transmission Project
VI. The Record Does Not Prove Present Need for Import Path 2 by 2030
VII. The Applicants Failed to Quantify Need and Benefit
VIII. ERCOT Forecast Reliability and Speculative Load Concerns
IX. Alternatives Were Not Fairly Evaluated
X. Public Meeting Notice Failures Under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)
XI. The Approximately 1,400 Landowners Added After Public Meetings
XII. Current County Tax Roll Failures and Late Application Notice
XIII. 180-Day Schedule, Due Process, and Fundamental Fairness
XIV. Habitable Structure Errors, Travel Trailers, and Route Scoring
XV. Prudent Avoidance, Schools, Churches, Homes, and Human Exposure
XVI. Community Values and Public Participation
XVII. QA/QC, GIS, Parcel, Field Verification, Floodplain, and Environmental Deficiencies
XVIII. Route Development Deficiencies
XIX. Response to Applicants Initial Post-Hearing Brief
XX. Proposed Findings of Fact
XXI. Proposed Conclusions of Law
XXII. Prayer for Relief
I. INTRODUCTION AND REQUESTED RELIEF
The State of Texas is being asked to approve one of the largest transmission line projects ever brought before the State Office of Administrative Hearings and the Public Utility Commission by Applicants that have failed in so many areas within this proceeding. The requested authority is not ordinary. It includes the ability to permanently take, strip, and scar thousands of acres of private land with a 765-kV transmission corridor.  It clears large easements thru the Texas hill country, change rural communities in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson counties, impose $100 billion cost on Texas ratepayers, and use eminent domain if landowners don’t agree.
That authority cannot be granted on assumptions and opinions. It cannot be granted on questionable planning document.  It cannot be granted because the Applicants are large utilities corporations with experienced high-powered lawyers and experts. It can only be granted if the Applicants prove, by substantial evidence in this record, that the certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public and that the proposed routes satisfy PURA and the Commission rules.
I respectfully request that the ALJs recommend denial of the Application.  At a minimum, no approved route should include property of any landowner who was denied a meaningful public meeting opportunity or received application notice so late that meaningful participation was impaired.
This requested relief is not extreme.  It is required before the State of Texas gives a private company authority to take private property from the citizens of Texas.
II. GOVERNING STANDARDS UNDER PURA AND THE COMMISSION RULES
PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to decide whether a certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. The statute requires consideration of the adequacy of existing service, the need for additional service, the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient and other utilities, and community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers, renewable-energy factors where applicable, and whether the line is needed to interconnect a transmission-service customer or end-use customer. See PURA § 37.056(c).
16 TAC § 25.101 reinforces that standard. It states that a certificate will issue only if the Commission finds the certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public and complies with PURA § 37.056. It also requires that transmission lines be routed, to the extent reasonable, to moderate the impact on affected communities and landowners, unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).
The Commission rule further requires consideration of whether routes parallel existing compatible rights-of-way, whether routes parallel other compatible rights-of-way such as roads and railroads, whether routes parallel property lines or natural or cultural features, and whether routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iv).
Prudent avoidance is not a slogan. It is defined in 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(6) as the limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort. That definition matters. It requires a real analysis of exposure, money, effort, and reasonable alternatives. A raw count of habitable structures within 500 feet does not by itself prove prudent avoidance.  The applicants’ approach does not count for actual human lives that reside in these habitable structures.  A school is different than a church. A church is different than a house. A house is different than a travel trailer.  
Notice is governed by 16 TAC § 22.52. Under § 22.52(a)(3), the applicant must mail notice of its application, on the filing date, to owners of land as stated on the current county tax rolls who would be directly affected.  Current is defined as “being used in the present time not from a year ago”.   Under § 22.52(a)(4), the utility must hold at least one public meeting before filing its application if 25 or more persons would be entitled to direct mail notice. The Applicants substantial increase of the scope of this project by adding 400 miles and 1,400 new affected landowners is why the Commission must follow the true intent of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) and protect the public’s interest.  Direct mail notice of that public meeting must be sent to affected owners on current county tax rolls. Under § 22.52(a)(5), failure to provide notice in accordance with the rule is cause for day-for-day extension of deadlines for intervention and Commission action.
These rules are not technicalities. They are how ordinary landowners learn that their land may be taken or burdened. They are how the Commission receives local information about homes, schools, churches, cemeteries, wells, stock tanks, pipelines, floodplains, ranching operations, historic resources, and community values. If the notice and public meeting process is defective, the route development process is defective too.
III. THE APPLICANTS STILL BEAR THE BURDEN OF PROOF
The Applicants actions are as if the burden of proof is with the landowners to disprove need, disprove routing, disprove notice, or disprove prudent avoidance. That is backwards. The burden belongs to the Applicants. Landowners are not required to design a better route. Landowners are not required to prove ERCOT wrong. Landowners are not required to show how the Applicants continuously misrepresent HB5066.  Landowners are not required to prove every Applicant failure. The Applicants must prove their application satisfies PURA and the Commission rules. They have not.
That burden is especially important here because the Applicants are asking for extraordinary authority for eminent domain on thousands of acres. They are asking the State to approve a new 765-kV transmission line across private land right thru the Texas Hill Country. They are asking to permanently scar properties, ranches, homes, schools, churches, and communities.  This ask requires more than generalized statements about reliability.
The Applicants cannot satisfy that burden by pointing to an administrative sufficiency order. Administrative sufficiency is not a final merits determination that every affected landowner received the required public meeting opportunity, that every tax roll was current, that every habitable structure was correctly identified, that community values were properly evaluated, or that prudent avoidance was performed. It means only that the case proceeded to maintain a 180-day schedule. The merits question remains.
The Applicants also cannot satisfy their burden by saying ERCOT or the Texas Legislators recommended the PBRP and that HB 5066 mandates Import Path 2.  ERCOT and the Texas Legislators are not the Commission. ERCOT and the Texas Legislators do not decide this CCN. The Commission must decide whether the Applicants proved this specific project is necessary.
IV. REPLY TO THE JOINT TSPS RESPONSE TO THE LEGISLATOR’S AMICUS BRIEF
The Joint TSPs response to the brief of certain Texas Legislators confirms the central problem with the Applicants case. They treat the 2024 PBRP as if it ends the proof the need argument. They argue that ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission spent almost two years studying reliability needs and that the Signatories now ask the Commission to set aside HB 5066. That is not a fair statement of the issue.
The legislators did not ask the Commission to ignore reliability. They asked the Commission to take care before locking Texas into a 765-kV buildout with extraordinary cost and property-rights consequences. Their brief states that ERCOTs PBRP raises serious concerns about whether the proposed plan is consistent with legislative direction and whether it appropriately prioritizes reliable, cost-effective energy solutions for Texans. Those concerns go directly to need.
The TSPs say the evidence establishes the need for the 765-kV import paths. But repeating that conclusion does not answer the specific gaps in this docket. It does not identify the exact MW deficiency at Big Hill. It does not identify the exact MW deficiency at Sand Lake. It does not quantify the specific MW benefit of the Bell County East to Big Hill segment. It does not reconcile the 2030 claim of need for Import Path 2 with actual evidence reflecting Import Path 2 needed in 2038. It does not prove that local generation or other alternatives were tested and rejected.
The TSPs also argue that deferral is inconsistent with PURA. I disagree. PURA requires a lawful decision supported by substantial evidence. PURA does not require the Commission to approve a CCN on an incomplete record just because the schedule is compressed. The 180-day schedule is important, but it does not erase the Applicants burden, and it does not excuse defective notice, defective public meetings, defective tax-roll data, or an unquantified need showing.
The TSPs argue that HB 5066 requires a transmission reliability plan. That may be true in a general sense, but it does not mean HB 5066 required this specific 765-kV line, this specific route network, or a transmission-only solution. The Legislature directed the Commission and ERCOT to address reliability needs in the Permian Basin. It did not state that rural Central Texas landowners carry a 765-kV import corridor without an adequate showing of need, alternatives, notice, public participation, and prudent avoidance.
The TSPs argue that the Permian Basin needs more transmission capacity now. But the issue is not whether more transmission capacity may be needed somewhere in the Permian Basin. The issue is whether this Project has been proven necessary now. The record contains repeated arguments that Import Path 2, including the Bell County East to Big Hill component, is tied to 2038 need rather than a present 2030 necessity. The Applicants cannot answer that conflict by simply saying time is of the essence.
The phrase “time is of the essence” should not become a shortcut around the law. Time may be important, but so are notice, public participation, accurate data, and private property rights. A rushed decision is not the same thing as a reliable decision. The Commission should not treat speed as a substitute for proof.
The Joint TSP response also tries to frame the legislators brief as a policy disagreement outside the scope of the docket. That misses the point. Need is a statutory issue. Cost to ratepayers is a statutory issue. Whether alternatives could meet the need with less harm is a statutory issue. Whether the plan adds no new generation capacity while imposing enormous transmission cost and land impacts is directly relevant to the public interest. Those are not outside issues; they are the heart of PURA § 37.056.
The response from the TSPs therefore does not cure the defect. It proves why this case should not be approved on autopilot. The Applicants want the Commission to treat the PBRP as conclusive. The Commission should instead treat it as one piece of evidence and require the Applicants to prove the statutory elements in this docket.
V. HB 5066 DOES NOT MANDATE THIS 765-KV TRANSMISSION PROJECT
The Applicants repeatedly rely on HB 5066 as if it mandated this project. It did not. HB 5066 required a reliability plan for the Permian Basin region. It did not mandate Import Path 2. It did not mandate a 765-kV line from Bell County East to Big Hill to Sand Lake. It did not mandate that transmission be selected over generation, demand-side, behind-the-meter, or hybrid solutions.
This distinction matters because the Applicants wording has repeatedly misrepresented the statutory language into a transmission-only mandate. The evidence points out that HB 5066 speaks in terms of addressing capacity and reliability needs; it does not say the only way to do that is through long-distance 765-kV import transmission.
The legislator’s amicus brief reinforces that concern. Forty-three Texas legislators told the Commission that the PBRP raises serious questions about whether the proposed 765-kV buildout is consistent with legislative direction and whether it prioritizes reliable, cost-effective energy solutions. The Applicants response does not erase that concern. It proves the concern is real, because the Applicants continue to treat HB 5066 as if it forecloses alternatives.
The Commission should reject that interpretation. If the Legislature had intended to require these specific routes, these specific import paths, and this specific 765-kV transmission buildout, it could have said so. It did not. A statute directing reliability planning should not be transformed into a blank check for transmission corridors across Texas.

VI. THE RECORD DOES NOT PROVE PRESENT NEED FOR IMPORT PATH 2 BY 2030
The Applicants say the Project is needed by 2030. Testimony and evidence have shown that this is not that simple as ERCOT’s Dec 12, 2024, sequencing letter clearly indicates one of the three proposed Import Paths is not needed until 2038 rather than a present 2030 necessity. 
I am not asking the ALJs to find that this project could never be needed. I am asking the ALJs to find that the Applicants did not reconcile the conflict in the record and did not prove present urgency. There is a big difference between a project that might be useful in a future planning horizon and a project that must be approved now with eminent-domain consequences.
The Applicants rely on 2030 and 2038 load forecasts, thermal overloads, voltage instability, and reliability criteria. But the record still lacks a clear project-specific showing of what exact MW deficiency the Import Path solves, when that deficiency occurs, and why this path must be approved now rather than deferred until updated information and alternatives can be evaluated.
The Applicants cannot simply merge all PBRP import paths into one conclusion and then declare each individual CCN necessary. PURA requires the Commission to evaluate this Application. Import Path 2 must stand on its own record. It has not.
VII. THE APPLICANTS FAILED TO QUANTIFY NEED AND BENEFIT
As an engineer, this is one of the biggest problems I see. The Applicants ask for approval of a massive project, but they do not provide the kind of specific, quantifiable need and benefit that should be required before this kind of authority is granted.
The Application does not clearly identify the specific MW deficiency requiring correction at Big Hill. It does not clearly identify the specific MW import requirement at Sand Lake. It does not identify the precise amount of power available at Bell County East for this purpose. It does not identify the amount of power expected to flow across this line in the relevant planning years. It does not quantify the amount of reliability improvement provided by this segment in a way that allows a landowner, ALJ, or Commissioner to determine whether the burden-imposed needs solved.
The Applicants are required to describe the need for construction and state how the proposed project will address the need. Saying that ERCOT identified reliability violations is not the same as showing how this specific line quantitatively solves a specific deficiency. A project of this magnitude should not be approved on broad planning assumptions when the Applicants could have provided the numbers.
If the Applicants cannot identify the actual MW need, they cannot prove the proposed project addresses that need. If they cannot quantify the benefit, the Commission cannot weigh that benefit against cost, community values, private property impacts, environmental impacts, and prudent avoidance.
VIII. ERCOT FORECAST RELIABILITY AND SPECULATIVE LOAD CONCERNS
The forecast underlying the 2024 PBRP has been challenged throughout the process. Judy Graci explained that the load forecast relied heavily on transmission service provider officer letters rather than binding commitments, and that a major portion of the additional non-oil-and-gas load consisted of cryptocurrency mining load. The record also includes arguments that ERCOT has since adopted more conservative planning numbers and methods and that the 2024 PBRP forecast has not been retested under those methods.
This matters because a forecast or plan is only as reliable as its assumptions. A 765-kV line is not a temporary investment. It is a permanent transmission corridor with permanent land impacts. If the load is speculative, if large loads are supported only by letters instead of contracts, if cryptocurrency or data-center load change, and if updated planning numbers reduce the forecast, then the Commission should require updated validation before approving the CCN.
The Applicants response to the legislator’s brief says the need was thoroughly evaluated. But a prior evaluation using disputed assumptions and opinions does not end the matter. The Commission should ask whether the forecast remains valid today, whether actual load has materialized, whether Senate Bill 6 changed the treatment of speculative large loads, whether local generation has changed the planning picture, and whether Import Path 2 remains necessary now.
The answer on this record is not sufficiently proven. That is enough to deny or defer.
IX. ALTERNATIVES WERE NOT FAIRLY EVALUATED
The Applicants and Joint TSPs repeatedly say transmission lines are needed. But the evidence and testimony reflect alternatives were not evaluated. The legislator’s amicus brief, the Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF) report attached to it, raise the same common-sense point: transmission lines do not generate electricity. They move power. If the reliability concern is a lack of power near Permian load, then local dispatchable generation, behind-the-meter generation, off-grid generation, microgrids, demand-side tools, and hybrid solutions should be meaningfully evaluated before Texas commits to long-distance 765-kV corridors affecting thousands of acres of Texas.
The evidence does not show that generation-side, load-side, existing-corridor, or hybrid alternatives were fully evaluated and rejected. That is the problem. The Applicants may disagree that generation alone eliminates the need, but disagreement is not proof that alternatives were studied compared and rejected.
The Joint TSP response attempts to dismiss this as policy advocacy inconsistent with ERCOT market structure. But the Commission is not being asked to redesign ERCOT. It is being asked not to approve a permanent transmission corridor until the Applicants prove that less intrusive and more cost-effective alternatives cannot meet the same need.
The record does not contain that proof. A reliability classification may exempt the project from some economic tests, but it does not exempt the Applicants from PURA § 37.056 or from the duty to prove the project is necessary and reasonable.
X. PUBLIC MEETING NOTICE FAILURES UNDER 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)
The public meeting issue is one of the clearest failures by the Applicants. The Applicants held public meetings in June 2025. After those meetings, they added approximately 400 miles of new route links and expanded the affected properties from about 2,800 to about 4,200. Approximately 1,400 landowners were newly affected. No additional public meetings were held for those landowners.
Applicants respond by saying they held three public meetings even though the rule requires at least one. That answer misses the point. Three meetings for the wrong footprint and the wrong group of landowners does not satisfy the purpose of the rule. Public meetings exist so affected landowners can provide information before routes are fixed. They are not supposed to be a box checked before the route network is substantially changed.
16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires a public meeting if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application. The newly added approximately 1,400 landowners easily exceeded that threshold. The rule does not divide landowners into first-class and second-class groups based on when the utility decided to add their land to the route network. Landowners added after public meetings are still affected landowners. They are still entitled to meaningful participation.
Public participation cannot occur when affected landowners are not told the project affects them. The newly affected landowners lost the chance to identify homes, schools, churches, cemeteries, water wells, stock tanks, pipelines, floodplains, wildlife habitat, historic resources, community values, and better routing alternatives before the route network was narrowed and filed.
That failure harmed the record. The Commission calls on the public to provide critical information about their property. The Commission is now being asked to approve an application and select a route from a record missing the very local information public meetings are designed to obtain. 
Approving this application would be like issuing a certificate of occupancy for one-third of the owners of a skyscraper after discovering the blueprints were incomplete, the inspections were flawed.  
XI. THE APPROXIMATELY 1,400 LANDOWNERS ADDED AFTER PUBLIC MEETINGS
The approximately 1,400 landowners are not a side issue. They are central to whether this was fair and lawful. Those landowners did not get the same process as the approximately 2,800 landowners invited to the June 2025 public meetings. They were not given the same chance to understand the project early. They were not given the same chance to ask questions. They were not given the same chance to provide routing information before the routes were developed.
The Applicants cannot cure that failure by saying application notice was later mailed. Application notice after the route network is developed is not the same as public meeting notice before filing. One notice tells landowners a case has been filed. The other gives landowners a chance to help shape the case before it is filed. Those are different rights serving different purposes.
Kevin Kennedy requested that no approved route traverse route links added or modified after the public meetings where affected landowners did not receive project notice until the application filing. I agree with that relief. If the Commission will not deny the Application, then no route should be selected that crosses one of the landowners deprived of the public meeting process or who received application notice so late that meaningful participation was impaired.
That remedy is fair and practical.  It does not ask the Commission to punish the Applicants. It asks the Commission not to reward a process that left one-third of affected landowners outside the public meeting process.
XII. CURRENT COUNTY TAX ROLL FAILURES AND LATE APPLICATION NOTICE
16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) requires notice to directly affected landowners as stated on the current county tax rolls. The current tax roll requirement matters because land changes hands, homes are built, ownership records change, and outdated data produces notice failures.
The record contains evidence that the Applicants did not properly use current county tax rolls and that at least 27 landowners were not properly notified. Burnet County and Kevin Kennedy corroborated stale-data and non-notice concerns. My initial brief identifies landowners including Christine Thies and Shane Hoffman who did not receive application notice until June 1, 2026, approximately 67 days after the Application was filed.
By June 1, deadlines were already approaching or had passed, discovery was underway, experts and lawyers had already been retained by other parties, and strategic decisions had already been made. Notice at that point was not meaningful notice. It was notice after the meaningful opportunities had already narrowed or disappeared.
The Applicants are seeking eminent-domain authority. Notice is not just another box to check; Notice is not a paperwork requirement; Notice is the foundation on which every other procedural right rests. If notice is late, intervention, discovery, testimony, cross-examination, briefing, and route development are all impacted.
The Applicants point to affidavits and Staff sufficiency recommendations. But an affidavit that notices were sent to a list does not prove the list was current. And a sufficiency order entered early in the case does not cure evidence later developed showing stale data, missed landowners, and late notice.
XIII. 180-DAY SCHEDULE, DUE PROCESS, AND FUNDAMENTAL FAIRNESS
This case proceeded on a compressed 180-day schedule even though it is one of the largest and most complex transmission proceedings Texas has seen. That schedule created a serious imbalance of the “scales of justice” between the Applicants and ordinary landowners, especially those who received late notice or no public meeting notice.
The Applicants had years to prepare. They had powerful lawyers, high paid consultants, expert engineers, planners, environmental teams, and unlimited resources. Many landowners had only a few weeks. Many are pro se. Many are over 65 years old. Many do not understand PUC procedure. Many do not have the confidence to navigate on computers. Many could not get lawyers because specialized firms had already been retained by earlier-noticed landowners. The result was not a level playing field.
The compressed schedule also affected the quality of this process. Intervenors had limited time to review thousands of pages, inspect route data, identify missed habitable structures, analyze maps, prepare testimony, file exhibits, conduct discovery, and prepare cross-examination. The hearing was compressed, cross-examination was limited from 3 to 13 minutes, and initial and rebuttal briefings 1 and 2 weeks respectfully. This raises fairness concerns tied to the scale of the case and the compressed process. Even the most experience attorneys can not manage.  
The Applicants cannot use the 180-day schedule as a shield. If the record is incomplete because the process was compressed, the answer is do not approve. The public interest is not served by approving a permanent eminent-domain project on an incomplete and procedurally unfair record.
XIV. HABITABLE STRUCTURE ERRORS, TRAVEL TRAILERS, AND ROUTE SCORING
Habitable structure counts are central to the Applicants routing analysis. The Applicants themselves identify habitable structures as one of the most critical data points. The record shows those counts and classifications are unreliable.
16 TAC § 25.101(a)(3) defines habitable structures as structures normally inhabited by humans or intended to be inhabited by humans on a daily or regular basis, including dwellings, mobile homes, apartment buildings, commercial structures, industrial structures, business structures, churches, hospitals, nursing homes, and schools. This definition requires human judgment. It is not enough to count points on a map without verifying what the structure is, how it is used, and how many humans use it.
The Application failed to clearly disclose that travel trailers were included within the habitable-structure inventory. Travel trailers are not the same as houses or fixed mobile homes. They can be temporary, seasonal, movable, and not intended for daily or regular habitation. In rural Texas, most are utilized as a temporary deer stand.  If travel trailers were counted on some links but fixed homes, schools, churches, or new residences were missed or miscoded elsewhere, then the route comparisons are flawed and distorted.
The evidence includes specific concerns about missed or unaddressed structures, including schools, churches, homeschool locations, as an example the Shane Hoffman residence. If one structure was missed by the someone sitting in a cubicle in Dallas, Texas using the desktop method, every route comparison using the same method becomes suspect. This is not about one landowner seeking a better count; it is about whether the Commission can rely on the route scoring at all.
When the inputs are wrong, the output is unreliable. The Commission should not approve a route based on a corrupted habitable-structure inventory.
XV. PRUDENT AVOIDANCE, SCHOOLS, CHURCHES, HOMES, AND HUMAN EXPOSURE
Prudent avoidance is about people. It is not about structures as abstract objects. The purpose of identifying habitable structures is to understand where people live, work, worship, learn, and gather. A route does not satisfy prudent avoidance merely because it has a lower spreadsheet number if the actual route places a 765-kV line near schools, churches, homes, homeschool locations, or other places where people regularly gather.
The Applicants argue all filed routes comply with prudent avoidance and that Route 894 best balances the factors. But they never show how many humans will be impacted: they never adequately define the reasonable investments of money and effort they considered to limit exposure; they did not show a clear exposure-limiting analysis. they substituted a 500-foot data screen for the actual prudent-avoidance policy.
Robert Noland showed the problem clearly regarding Florence Elementary School and Link F34. He explained that Applicants overlooked the school and the future highway interchange, and that witness testimony showed schools should be avoided. PUC Staff witness John Poole reportedly explained that the purpose of avoiding habitable structures is avoiding human exposure, and that a school with hundreds of students should be considered in that light.
My own route concerns with G71, G72, and G73 involve homes, a homeschool environment, missing habitable structures, and real human exposure. The point is not fear. The point is that the Commission rule requires reasonable efforts to limit exposures that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort. If a slight route adjustment can reduce exposure to homes, schools, or churches without undermining reliability, that is exactly the kind of thing prudent avoidance requires the Applicants to evaluate.
The Applicants also rely on health testimony, but the record includes concerns that their expert had not researched EMF exposure or health impacts associated specifically with 765-kV transmission lines. That does not prove harm, but it also does not prove prudent avoidance. The burden is not on landowners to prove danger with certainty. 
XVI. COMMUNITY VALUES AND PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
Community values are not just comments placed in a file or checking another box. They are a statutory factor. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to consider community values. The Applicants say they considered public comments, but the record does not show that community values were meaningfully tabulated, ranked, weighed, compared, or incorporated into final route selection.
That problem is made worse by the approximately 1,400 landowners excluded from public meetings. Applicants repeatedly testified that public meetings are important for identifying community values. If that is true, then excluding one-third of affected landowners from that process means the community-values record is incomplete.
The initial briefs show community values across the study area: the Lampasas River watershed, wildlife management, multigenerational ranches, Salado Creek, historic Salado, schools, churches, cemeteries, oak trees, rural viewsheds, generational property, cattle operations, stock tanks, high-hazard pipeline areas, tribal ancestral lands and sacred sites, and the basic value of not unnecessarily fragmenting private property. These are not isolated complaints. They are the statutory record of community values.
The Applicants attempt to reduce these values to route-table factors. But community values are not reducible to miles and counts. The Commission must consider the human and community meaning of the land affected.

II. GOVERNING STANDARDS UNDER PURA AND THE COMMISSION RULES
PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to decide whether a certificate is necessary for the service,
accommodation, convenience, or safety ofthe public. The statute requires consideration ofthe adequacy
of existing service, the need for additional service, the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient
and other utilities, and community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values,
environmental integrity, probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers, renewable-
energy factors where applicable, and whether the line is needed to interconnect a transmission-service
customer or end-use customer. See PURA § 37.056(c).
 16 TAC § 25.101 reinforces that standard. It states that a certificate will issue only ifthe Commission
finds the certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public and
complies with PURA § 37.056. It also requires that transmission lines be routed, to the extent reasonable,
to moderate the impact on affected communities and landowners, unless grid reliability and security
dictate otherwise. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).
The Commission rule further requires consideration of whether routes parallel existing compatible rights-
of-way, whether routes parallel other compatible rights-of-way such as roads and railroads, whether
routes parallel property lines or natural or cultural features, and whether routes conform with the policy of
prudent avoidance. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iv).
Prudent avoidance is not a slogan. It is defined in 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(6) as the limiting of exposures to
electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort. That
definition matters. It requires a real analysis of exposure, money, effort, and reasonable alternatives. A
raw count of habitable structures within 500 feet does not by itself prove prudent avoidance. The
applicants' approach does not count for actual human lives that reside in these habitable structures. A
school is different than a church. A church is different than a house. A house is different than a travel
trailer.
 Notice is governed by 16 TAC § 22.52. Under § 22.52(a)(3), the applicant must mail notice of its
application, on the filing date, to owners of land as stated on the current county tax rolls who would be
directly affected. Current is defined as "being used in the present time not from a year ago" Under §
22.52(a)(4), the utility must hold at least one public meeting before filing its application if 25 or more
persons would be entitled to direct mail notice. The Applicants substantial increase ofthe scope ofthis
project by adding 400 miles and 1,400 new affected landowners is why the Commission must follow the
true intent of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) and protect the public's interest. Direct mail notice of that public
meeting must be sent to affected owners on current county tax rolls. Under § 22.52(a)(5), failure to
provide notice in accordance with the rule is cause for day-for-day extension of deadlines for intervention
and Commission action.
These rules are not technicalities. They are how ordinary landowners learn that their land may be taken or
burdened. They are how the Commission receives local information about homes, schools, churches,
cemeteries, wells, stock tanks, pipelines, floodplains, ranching operations, historic resources, and
community values. Ifthe notice and public meeting process is defective, the route development process is
defective too.

 The Applicants are required to describe the need for construction and state how the proposed project will
address the need. Saying that ERCOT identified reliability violations is not the same as showing how this
specific line quantitatively solves a specific deficiency. A project of this magnitude should not be
approved on broad planning assumptions when the Applicants could have provided the numbers.
Ifthe Applicants cannot identify the actual MW need, they cannot prove the proposed project addresses
that need. Ifthey cannot quantify the benefit, the Commission cannot weigh that benefit against cost,
community values, private property impacts, environmental impacts, and prudent avoidance.
VIII. ERCOT FORECAST RELIABILITY AND SPECULATIVE LOAD CONCERNS
The forecast underlying the 2024 PBRP has been challenged throughout the process. Judy Graci
explained that the load forecast relied heavily on transmission service provider officer letters rather than
binding commitments, and that a major portion ofthe additional non-oil-and-gas load consisted of
cryptocurrency mining load. The record also includes arguments that ERCOT has since adopted more
conservative planning numbers and methods and that the 2024 PBRP forecast has not been retested under
those methods.
This matters because a forecast or plan is only as reliable as its assumptions. A 765-kV line is not a
temporary investment. It is a permanent transmission corridor with permanent land impacts. Ifthe load is
speculative, if large loads are supported only by letters instead of contracts, if cryptocurrency or data-
center load change, and if updated planning numbers reduce the forecast, then the Commission should
require updated validation before approving the CCN.
The Applicants response to the legislator's brief says the need was thoroughly evaluated. But a prior
evaluation using disputed assumptions and opinions does not end the matter. The Commission should ask
whether the forecast remains valid today, whether actual load has materialized, whether Senate Bill 6
changed the treatment of speculative large loads, whether local generation has changed the planning
picture, and whether Import Path 2 remains necessary now.
The answer on this record is not sufficiently proven. That is enough to deny or defer.
IX. ALTERNATIVES WERE NOT FAIRLY EVALUATED
The Applicants and Joint TSPs repeatedly say transmission lines are needed. But the evidence and
testimony reflect alternatives were not evaluated. The legislator's amicus brief, the Texas Public Policy
Foundation (TPPF) report attached to it, raise the same common-sense point: transmission lines do not
generate electricity. They move power. Ifthe reliability concern is a lack of power near Permian load,
then local dispatchable generation, behind-the-meter generation, off-grid generation, microgrids, demand-
side tools, and hybrid solutions should be meaningfully evaluated before Texas commits to long-distance
765-kV corridors affecting thousands of acres of Texas.
The evidence does not show that generation-side, load-side, existing-corridor, or hybrid alternatives were
fully evaluated and rejected. That is the problem. The Applicants may disagree that generation alone
eliminates the need, but disagreement is not proofthat alternatives were studied compared and rejected.
The Joint TSP response attempts to dismiss this as policy advocacy inconsistent with ERCOT market
structure. But the Commission is not being asked to redesign ERCOT. It is being asked not to approve a
permanent transmission corridor until the Applicants prove that less intrusive and more cost-effective
alternatives cannot meet the same need.
 The record does not contain that proof. A reliability classification may exempt the project from some
economic tests, but it does not exempt the Applicants from PURA § 37.056 or from the duty to prove the
project is necessary and reasonable.
X. PUBLIC MEETING NOTICE FAILURES UNDER 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)
The public meeting issue is one ofthe clearest failures by the Applicants. The Applicants held public
meetings in June 2025. After those meetings, they added approximately 400 miles of new route links and
expanded the affected properties from about 2,800 to about 4,200. Approximately 1,400 landowners were
newly affected. No additional public meetings were held for those landowners.
Applicants respond by saying they held three public meetings even though the rule requires at least one.
That answer misses the point. Three meetings for the wrong footprint and the wrong group of landowners
does not satisfy the purpose ofthe rule. Public meetings exist so affected landowners can provide
information before routes are fixed. They are not supposed to be a box checked before the route network
is substantially changed.
 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires a public meeting if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct
mail notice of the application. The newly added approximately 1,400 landowners easily exceeded that
threshold. The rule does not divide landowners into first-class and second-class groups based on when the
utility decided to add their land to the route network. Landowners added after public meetings are still
affected landowners. They are still entitled to meaningful participation.
Public participation cannot occur when affected landowners are not told the project affects them. The
newly affected landowners lost the chance to identify homes, schools, churches, cemeteries, water wells,
stock tanks, pipelines, floodplains, wildlife habitat, historic resources, community values, and better
routing alternatives before the route network was narrowed and filed.
That failure harmed the record. The Commission calls on the public to provide critical information about
their property. The Commission is now being asked to approve an application and select a route from a
record missing the very local information public meetings are designed to obtain.
Approving this application would be like issuing a certificate of occupancy for one-third of the owners of
a skyscraper after discovering the blueprints were incomplete, the inspections were flawed.
XI. THE APPROXIMATELY 1,400 LANDOWNERS ADDED AFTER PUBLIC MEETINGS
The approximately 1,400 landowners are not a side issue. They are central to whether this was fair and
lawful. Those landowners did not get the same process as the approximately 2,800 landowners invited to
the June 2025 public meetings. They were not given the same chance to understand the project early.
They were not given the same chance to ask questions. They were not given the same chance to provide
routing information before the routes were developed.
The Applicants cannot cure that failure by saying application notice was later mailed. Application notice
after the route network is developed is not the same as public meeting notice before filing. One notice
tells landowners a case has been filed. The other gives landowners a chance to help shape the case before
it is filed. Those are different rights serving different purposes.
Kevin Kennedy requested that no approved route traverse route links added or modified after the public
meetings where affected landowners did not receive project notice until the application filing. I agree with
that relief. Ifthe Commission will not deny the Application, then no route should be selected that crosses
one ofthe landowners deprived of the public meeting process or who received application notice so late
that meaningful participation was impaired.
 That remedy is fair and practical. It does not ask the Commission to punish the Applicants. It asks the
Commission not to reward a process that left one-third of affected landowners outside the public meeting
process.
XII. CURRENT COUNTY TAX ROLL FAILURES AND LATE APPLICATION NOTICE
16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) requires notice to directly affected landowners as stated on the current county tax
rolls. The current tax roll requirement matters because land changes hands, homes are built, ownership
records change, and outdated data produces notice failures.
The record contains evidence that the Applicants did not properly use current county tax rolls and that at
least 27 landowners were not properly notified. Burnet County and Kevin Kennedy corroborated stale-
data and non-notice concerns. My initial brief identifies landowners including Christine Thies and Shane
Hoffman who did not receive application notice until June 1,2026, approximately 67 days after the
Application was filed.
By June 1, deadlines were already approaching or had passed, discovery was underway, experts and
lawyers had already been retained by other parties, and strategic decisions had already been made. Notice
at that point was not meaningful notice. It was notice after the meaningful opportunities had already
narrowed or disappeared.
The Applicants are seeking eminent-domain authority. Notice is not just another box to check; Notice is
not a paperwork requirement; Notice is the foundation on which every other procedural right rests. If
notice is late, intervention, discovery, testimony, cross-examination, briefing, and route development are
all impacted.
The Applicants point to affidavits and Staff sufficiency recommendations. But an affidavit that notices
were sent to a list does not prove the list was current. And a sufficiency order entered early in the case
does not cure evidence later developed showing stale data, missed landowners, and late notice.
XIII. 180-DAY SCHEDULE, DUE PROCESS, AND FUNDAMENTAL FAIRNESS
This case proceeded on a compressed 180-day schedule even though it is one ofthe largest and most
complex transmission proceedings Texas has seen. That schedule created a serious imbalance of the
"scales ofjustice" between the Applicants and ordinary landowners, especially those who received late
notice or no public meeting notice.
The Applicants had years to prepare. They had powerful lawyers, high paid consultants, expert engineers,
planners, environmental teams, and unlimited resources. Many landowners had only a few weeks. Many
are pro se. Many are over 65 years old. Many do not understand PUC procedure. Many do not have the
confidence to navigate on computers. Many could not get lawyers because specialized firms had already
been retained by earlier-noticed landowners. The result was not a level playing field.
The compressed schedule also affected the quality ofthis process. Intervenors had limited time to review
thousands of pages, inspect route data, identify missed habitable structures, analyze maps, prepare
testimony, file exhibits, conduct discovery, and prepare cross-examination. The hearing was compressed,
cross-examination was limited from 3 to 13 minutes, and initial and rebuttal briefings 1 and 2 weeks
respectfully. This raises fairness concerns tied to the scale of the case and the compressed process. Even
the most experience attorneys can not manage.
The Applicants cannot use the 180-day schedule as a shield. Ifthe record is incomplete because the
process was compressed, the answer is do not approve. The public interest is not served by approving a
permanent eminent-domain project on an incomplete and procedurally unfair record.
 XIV. HABITABLE STRUCTURE ERRORS, TRAVEL TRAILERS, AND ROUTE SCORING
Habitable structure counts are central to the Applicants routing analysis. The Applicants themselves
identify habitable structures as one of the most critical data points. The record shows those counts and
classifications are unreliable.
 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(3) defines habitable structures as structures normally inhabited by humans or
intended to be inhabited by humans on a daily or regular basis, including dwellings, mobile homes,
apartment buildings, commercial structures, industrial structures, business structures, churches, hospitals,
nursing homes, and schools. This definition requires human judgment. It is not enough to count points on
a map without verifying what the structure is, how it is used, and how many humans use it.
The Application failed to clearly disclose that travel trailers were included within the habitable-structure
inventory. Travel trailers are not the same as houses or fixed mobile homes. They can be temporary,
seasonal, movable, and not intended for daily or regular habitation. In rural Texas, most are utilized as a
temporary deer stand. Iftravel trailers were counted on some links but fixed homes, schools, churches, or
new residences were missed or miscoded elsewhere, then the route comparisons are flawed and distorted.
The evidence includes specific concerns about missed or unaddressed structures, including schools,
churches, homeschool locations, as an example the Shane Hoffman residence. If one structure was missed
by the someone sitting in a cubicle in Dallas, Texas using the desktop method, every route comparison
using the same method becomes suspect. This is not about one landowner seeking a better count; it is
about whether the Commission can rely on the route scoring at all.
When the inputs are wrong, the output is unreliable. The Commission should not approve a route based
on a corrupted habitable-structure inventory.
XV. PRUDENT AVOIDANCE, SCHOOLS, CHURCHES, HOMES, AND HUMAN EXPOSURE
Prudent avoidance is about people. It is not about structures as abstract objects. The purpose of
identifying habitable structures is to understand where people live, work, worship, learn, and gather. A
route does not satisfy prudent avoidance merely because it has a lower spreadsheet number if the actual
route places a 765-kV line near schools, churches, homes, homeschool locations, or other places where
people regularly gather.
The Applicants argue all filed routes comply with prudent avoidance and that Route 894 best balances the
factors. But they never show how many humans will be impacted: they never adequately define the
reasonable investments of money and effort they considered to limit exposure; they did not show a clear
exposure-limiting analysis. they substituted a 500-foot data screen for the actual prudent-avoidance
policy.
Robert Noland showed the problem clearly regarding Florence Elementary School and Link F34. He
explained that Applicants overlooked the school and the future highway interchange, and that witness
testimony showed schools should be avoided. PUC Staffwitness John Poole reportedly explained that the
purpose of avoiding habitable structures is avoiding human exposure, and that a school with hundreds of
students should be considered in that light.
My own route concerns with G71, G72, and G73 involve homes, a homeschool environment, missing
habitable structures, and real human exposure. The point is not fear. The point is that the Commission rule
requires reasonable efforts to limit exposures that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money
and effort. If a slight route adjustment can reduce exposure to homes, schools, or churches without
undermining reliability, that is exactly the kind of thing prudent avoidance requires the Applicants to
evaluate.
 The Applicants also rely on health testimony, but the record includes concerns that their expert had not
researched EMF exposure or health impacts associated specifically with 765-kV transmission lines. That
does not prove harm, but it also does not prove prudent avoidance. The burden is not on landowners to
prove danger with certainty.
XVI. COMMUNITY VALUES AND PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
Community values are not just comments placed in a file or checking another box. They are a statutory
factor. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to consider community values. The Applicants say they
considered public comments, but the record does not show that community values were meaningfully
tabulated, ranked, weighed, compared, or incorporated into final route selection.
That problem is made worse by the approximately 1,400 landowners excluded from public meetings.
Applicants repeatedly testified that public meetings are important for identifying community values. If
that is true, then excluding one-third of affected landowners from that process means the community-
values record is incomplete.
The initial briefs show community values across the study area: the Lampasas River watershed, wildlife
management, multigenerational ranches, Salado Creek, historic Salado, schools, churches, cemeteries,
oak trees, rural viewsheds, generational property, cattle operations, stock tanks, high-hazard pipeline
areas, tribal ancestral lands and sacred sites, and the basic value of not unnecessarily fragmenting private
property. These are not isolated complaints. They are the statutory record of community values.
The Applicants attempt to reduce these values to route-table factors. But community values are not
reducible to miles and counts. The Commission must consider the human and community meaning ofthe
land affected.
XVII. QA/QC, GIS, PARCEL, FIELD VERIFICATION, FLOODPLAIN, PIPELINE, AND
ENVIRONMENTAL DEFICIENCIES
A project this large required extraordinary quality control. The record instead shows repeated data
problems: stale tax rolls, missed landowners, late notices, missed structures, travel trailer classification
issues, school and church concerns, pipeline crossing and paralleling concerns, floodplain and drainage
concerns, stock tank impacts, environmental survey limitations, and route changes after public meetings.
These errors are not isolated. They are connected. Stale tax rolls affect notice. Bad notice affects public
participation. Missing public participation affects community values and route development. Missed
structures affect prudent avoidance. Unverified field data affects environmental integrity and routing. Bad
route inputs affect the final route recommendation.
The Applicants ask the Commission to trust their route data. The record gives the Commission reason not
to. Before approving a 765-kV line with eminent-domain consequences, the Commission should require
corrected data and a transparent QA/QC showing.
XVIII. ROUTE DEVELOPMENT DEFICIENCIES
The route development process was not just broad; it was flawed. The Applicants added, removed, and
modified hundreds of miles of route links after the public meetings. That means many affected
landowners never had a chance to comment on the routes that affected them before those routes became
part ofthe filed Application.
Route 894 may be the Applicants preferred route, but preference is not proof. A route can only be selected
if it is supported by reliable data and satisfies the statutory factors. If the data is flawed, if notice was
 defective, if community values are incomplete, and if prudent avoidance was not properly performed,
then the recommendation cannot stand.
XIX. RESPONSE TO APPLICANTS INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
The Applicants Initial Brief treats the major issues as settled. They are not.
First, the Applicants say the Application is adequate because it included 122 routes, 171 links, cost
estimates, need documentation, environmental assessment material, engineering support, and notice
information. Quantity is not the same as adequacy. Many routes do not cure defective notice, stale tax
rolls, missed structures, or an unquantified need showing.
Second, the Applicants say public meetings and notices satisfied 16 TAC § 22.52. That argument ignores
the approximately 400 miles of route links added after the public meetings and the approximately 1,400
landowners denied public meeting participation. It also ignores evidence of stale tax rolls and late notice.
Third, the Applicants say Staffand the ALJs found notice sufficient. That does not resolve the merits.
Early sufficiency findings cannot cure later-developed evidence that landowners were missed, late
noticed, or excluded from the public meeting process.
Fourth, the Applicants say the 2024 PBRP and HB 5066 establish need. They do not. HB 5066 required
reliability planning; it did not mandate this line. ERCOT planning is important; it is not a substitute for
the Applicants burden in this CCN application.
Fifth, the Applicants say the Project is needed by 2030. The record contains substantial contrary
arguments tying Import Path 2 to 2038 and showing the Applicants did not reconcile the timing conflict.
The safe, lawful conclusion is denial or deferral until the timing is reconciled.
Sixth, the Applicants say all routes comply with prudent avoidance. But they did not demonstrate the
reasonable investments ofmoney and effort considered to limit exposure. They relied on structure counts
that the record shows are unreliable.
Seventh, the Applicants say Route 894 is their preferred route and no other better route was proven. That
recommendation has no validity as it has been shown in this record that the data used is flawed.
For those reasons, the Applicants Initial Brief confirms the weaknesses in their case. It relies on
conclusions, sufficiency orders, generalized ERCOT planning, and route tables. It does not answer the
core failures in this record.

XXI. PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. The Commission has jurisdiction over this proceeding under PURA.
2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the conduct of the hearing.
3. The Applicants bear the burden to prove the Application satisfies PURA § 37.056 and the Commission
rules.
4. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to consider need, adequacy of existing service, probable
improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers, community values, recreational and park areas,
historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and other statutory factors.
5. 16 TAC § 25.101 requires the Commission to grant a certificate only if it finds the certificate necessary
for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public and compliant with PURA § 37.056.
 6. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires transmission lines to be routed, to the extent reasonable, to
moderate the impact on affected communities and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate
otherwise.
7. 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(6) defines prudent avoidance as the limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic
fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.
8. 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) requires application notice to directly affected landowners as stated on current
county tax rolls.
9. 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires at least one public meeting prior to filing if 25 or more persons would
be entitled to direct mail notice of the application.
10. 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(5) provides that failure to provide notice in accordance with the rule is cause for
day-for-day extension of deadlines for intervention and Commission action.
11. An administrative sufficiency finding does not relieve the Applicants of their ultimate burden to prove
compliance with PURA and the Commission rules on the merits.
12. ERCOT planning documents and Commission actions in related projects do not relieve the Applicants
of their burden to prove this specific CCN Application in this docket.
13. HB 5066 does not mandate approval ofthis specific project or any specific route.
14. The Applicants failed to prove a sufficiently quantified project-specific need and benefit for the Bell
County East to Big Hill segment.
15. The Applicants failed to reconcile the record conflict concerning whether Import Path 2 is needed by
